passages.happening:
The man brought Ezekiel to the gate facing east, ‘and I saw the glory of the God of Israel coming from the east. His voice was like the roar of many waters, and the earth shone with His glory’ (verse 2). It was like the visions he had seen when God came to destroy the city and by the River Kebar, and Ezekiel fell on his face (verse 3). ‘And the glory of the LORD entered the temple through the gate facing east’ (verse 4). The Spirit lifted him into the inner court, ‘and the glory of the LORD filled the temple’ (verse 5).

A voice spoke from the temple: ‘Son of man, this is the place of My throne and the place for the soles of My feet, where I will dwell among the Israelites forever’ (verse 7). The house of Israel and its kings will never again defile his name with their idols and with the dead of their kings beside his house (verses 7-9). Ezekiel is to describe the temple to the people, ‘so that they may be ashamed of their iniquities’ (verse 10). ‘This is the law of the temple: All its surrounding territory on top of the mountain will be most holy’ (verse 12).
passages.hearers:
This is the turning point of the whole book. The glory that left the temple toward the east in chapters 10 and 11 returns from the east and fills the house again.

In the ancient world, the arrival of a god's presence, often as a statue, made a building a temple. Israel had no statue. The glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle and Solomon's temple at their dedication, and Ezekiel's vision follows that pattern: the building is measured and finished, but it is not a temple until the glory enters.

Solomon built his palace right beside the temple, so that the king's house and God's house shared a wall, and later kings brought idolatry into the courts. The phrase about the kings' funeral offerings is disputed; the Hebrew word usually means corpses. In every reading, royal power and its rites had crowded in on God's holy space.
passages.later: At Solomon's temple ‘the glory of the LORD filled the house of the LORD’ (1 Kings 8:11). At the tabernacle ‘the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle’ (Exodus 40:34).
passages.asks: The glory came back to the place it had left. Ask where you have felt God's absence. And ask what it would mean to make room for his return.

passages.happening: The man gave the measurements of the altar: a stepped structure rising from a base in stages, with horns at its corners and steps on its east side (verses 13-17). Then God gave the rules for its consecration. For seven days the priests of Zadok's line are to offer a young bull and a goat as sin offerings, with burnt offerings, to make atonement for the altar and cleanse it (verses 18-26). ‘At the end of these days, from the eighth day on, the priests are to present your burnt offerings and peace offerings on the altar. Then I will accept you, declares the Lord GOD’ (verse 27).
passages.hearers:
The altar rose some ten or eleven long cubits, roughly five to six meters. Some scholars compare its terraced shape to the temple towers of Babylon, which Ezekiel would have seen; others see an enlargement of Israel's own great altars. Its seven days of consecration follow the pattern of Moses' consecration of the tabernacle altar and priests.

In Ezekiel's day people had worshiped the sun at the temple, facing east with their backs to the sanctuary. In the new temple the altar's steps face east, so the priest going up faces west, toward God's house. The horns were projections at the corners where blood was applied.
passages.later: The tabernacle altar was consecrated for seven days and made most holy (Exodus 29:37). Moses ordained Aaron and his sons over seven days (Leviticus 8:33).
passages.hard:
Why does Ezekiel's future temple have animal sacrifices, when the New Testament says Christ's sacrifice ended them?

Hebrews teaches that Christ ‘offered for all time one sacrifice for sins’ (Hebrews 10:12). Readers relate this to Ezekiel 43 in several ways, and this site takes no side. Dispensational interpreters who expect a literal future temple hold that its sacrifices will not take away sin, which Christ alone does, but will serve as memorials looking back to the cross, or as means of ceremonial purity where God's presence dwells. Many other Christians read the sacrifices as the prophet describing future worship in the only terms his hearers could understand, so that the vision's point, full atonement and acceptance before God, is fulfilled in Christ, the church and the new creation. Others read chapters 40 to 48 as a program offered to the returning exiles, whose sacrifices belonged to the old covenant still in force then. Jewish readers take the sacrifices as part of the worship of a future temple.

Christians agree on the first-order point: Christ's death is the full and final atonement for sin. How Ezekiel's vision relates to it is a second-order question. The vision makes no claim about any modern temple.
passages.asks: The chapter ends with God's promise to accept his people. Ask whether you live as someone God has accepted. And ask what it cost for that acceptance to be given.
